title: Is your AI feature working? Usage is not the same as value
description: Clicks and messages show that people are trying it. To know whether AI helps, measure quality, task outcomes and guardrail signals.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: flows where models, automations and human review work together, with quality criteria defined by the team.

blocks.text: It's tempting to evaluate an artificial intelligence feature by looking at how many people click on it, how many messages they send or how many times they come back to use it.
Those numbers are useful. But on their own, they don't answer the most important question: is the feature helping people reach a better outcome?

Someone might try an AI feature out of curiosity and never come back. Someone else might use it only a few times, but save time on an important task. If we only measure usage volume, we risk confusing novelty with value.
Start with the job the person wants to get done

Before choosing metrics, describe the task the feature is meant to improve. In a customer support product, for example, AI might summarize a conversation, suggest a reply or classify a request. Each action has a different purpose and needs its own criteria.

items: If the AI summarizes conversations, evaluate whether the person understands the case faster and whether the summary leaves out critical information.
If it suggests replies, look at how often suggestions are accepted, edited or discarded, but also at the quality of the final reply.
If it classifies requests, evaluate accuracy, the number of human corrections and the impact on resolution time.

blocks.text: The metric needs to be tied to the real work, not just to the presence of AI in the interface.
Build a metric tree
A useful structure separates four dimensions:
do people find the feature and manage to complete their first task?
is the output correct, useful, relevant and understandable?
does the task get faster, simpler or more reliable? Does the person have to correct the output a lot?

blocks.lead: Outcome for the business and risk:
blocks.text: is there an impact on retention, operating cost or service quality? Do errors, rework, complaints or support needs go up?
This tree keeps the team from celebrating a high number of generations without checking whether the output was actually used.
Measure human correction too

In AI experiences, behavior after the generation matters a lot. A reply copied without changes may indicate usefulness, but it may also mean the person didn't notice a mistake. A heavily edited reply may mean the feature helped them get started but still requires a lot of work. A rejected reply may reveal low relevance, lack of trust or simply that the person wanted to explore another option.

Read the signals together. Combine product events with quality samples reviewed by people, contextual feedback, usability tests and task analysis. Define quality criteria before looking at the results so you don't judge the AI only by what sounds convincing.
Include guardrail metrics
A feature can cut the time a task takes and still introduce risks. A suggested reply can speed up support but increase incorrect information or inappropriate messages.

Choose guardrail metrics that fit the context: correction rate, escalation to a person, critical errors, complaints, rework or abandonment. Not all of them will be relevant to every product. What matters is deciding before launch which signals would tell you the optimization is hurting the experience.
Compare against a baseline

Without a baseline, it's hard to say whether things improved. Before launching, record how the task works today: time to complete, success rate, number of errors, satisfaction or perceived effort. Then compare carefully, taking into account differences in audience, complexity and frequency of use.

When it's possible and appropriate, run controlled tests. When it isn't, combine before-and-after analysis with qualitative research and be transparent about the limitations. Behavior can change with new model versions, new contexts and different types of requests. Ongoing monitoring and evaluation are part of the product.
The question isn't just whether people use the AI. It's whether it helps them do the job it was built for, better.
